 Advertisement Home / Legal News / Gravity of economic offence alone cannot justify indefinite custody after probe ends: High Court Gravity of economic offence alone cannot justify indefinite custody after probe ends: High Court
 The court grants regular bail in an alleged organised investment fraud involving thousands of investors, noting that the trial is unlikely to conclude in the foreseeable future
 Saurabh Malik 
 Tribune News Service 
 Chandigarh, Updated At : 06:59 PM Nov 16, 2026 IST 
 Follow us Connect with us Justice Sumeet Goel held that prolonged incarceration and the likely delay in the conclusion of the trial were relevant considerations, even in cases where the prosecution had alleged the existence of an organised fraudulent investment network. iStock photo Advertisement The seriousness of allegations in a money laundering case cannot be the sole ground for keeping an accused in custody indefinitely, particularly when the investigation is complete and the trial is unlikely to conclude in the foreseeable future, the Punjab and Haryana High Court has ruled while granting regular bail to an accused in an alleged organised investment fraud “involving thousands of innocent investors”.
 Justice Sumeet Goel held that prolonged incarceration and the likely delay in the conclusion of the trial were relevant considerations, even in cases where the prosecution had alleged the existence of an organised fraudulent investment network.
 “The seriousness of the allegations, though an important consideration, cannot be the sole ground for keeping an accused in custody for an indefinite period, particularly when the investigation has been completed,” the court observed.
 Appearing on behalf of the petitioner, senior advocate Bipan Ghai, along with counsel Nikhil Ghai, argued that the petitioner had been falsely implicated in the case and that his continued incarceration was not warranted in the factual circumstances of the case.
 Advertisement 
 The Enforcement Directorate (ED) had opposed Harinder Pal Singh’s bail plea, contending that the allegations against the petitioner were “serious in nature and relate to a large-scale organised investment fraud involving thousands of innocent investors”.
 The ED further submitted that the investigation “revealed that the petitioner, along with his associate, operated under the name of ID ‘Singh Brothers’ and was instrumental in bringing a large number of investors and sub-agents into the scheme”.
 Justice Goel observed: “Indubitably, the prosecution has alleged the existence of an organised fraudulent investment network in which innocent persons were allegedly induced to part with their hard-earned money on the false promise of assured returns from foreign exchange trading. The allegations regarding the diversion of funds through different entities, generation of proceeds of crime and acquisition of properties in India and abroad are matters which would require proper examination/adjudication during the course of trial”.
 Advertisement 
 Justice Goel noted that the petitioner was arrested on September 17, 2025, and had remained in judicial custody for approximately one year and two months. The ED had filed its prosecution complaint on November 14, 2025, followed by a supplementary complaint on February 2, 2026.
 Justice Goel also took note of the “stage of proceedings before the trial Court”. The prosecution proposes to examine 49 witnesses and has relied upon 147 documents running into more than 12,400 pages, while the case is admittedly still at the pre-cognisance stage.
 Justice Goel added: “Given the magnitude of prosecution evidence, it is evident that the trial is not likely to conclude within the foreseeable future. The petitioner cannot be expected to remain incarcerated for an indefinite period merely because the allegations relate to an economic offence. Thus, the prolonged incarceration, coupled with the absence of a reasonable possibility of the trial concluding within a foreseeable period, cannot be ignored while considering a prayer for bail”.
 Advertisement 
 The court also noted that the prosecution case was substantially based on documentary evidence, bank account transactions, electronic records, statements recorded under Section 50 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act and property-related documents. The investigation qua the petitioner stood concluded, with no further custodial interrogation shown to be necessary.
 Finding no tangible material to suggest that the petitioner was likely to abscond, evade the process of law or influence prosecution witnesses, the court observed that the apprehension of witness interference remained unsupported by substantive material.
 Taking these circumstances into consideration, the High Court allowed the petition and directed the petitioner’s release on regular bail, subject to terms and conditions to be determined by the competent court.
